title: Cheat Sheet - Routines
markdown:
When a program calls one of these and does not define it itself, the website adds its code to the end of the program before assembling. They follow the System V calling convention: arguments in `rdi`, `rsi`; result in `rax`; `rbx`, `rbp`, `rsp` and `r12` to `r15` are kept, everything else may change.

| Routine | Arguments | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `print_str` | `rdi` = address of a zero-terminated string | prints it |
| `print_char` | `dil` = a character | prints it |
| `print_newline` | | prints a new line |
| `print_int` | `rdi` = a signed number | prints it in decimal |
| `print_uint` | `rdi` = an unsigned number | prints it in decimal |
| `print_hex` | `rdi` = a number | prints `0x` and lower-case hex digits |
| `print_bin` | `rdi` = a number, `rsi` = bits (1 to 64) | prints that many of its lowest bits |
| `read_int` | | skips spaces and new lines, reads a whole number: `rax` = it, `rdx` = 1; at the end of the input both are 0 |
| `read_char` | | `rax` = the next character, or −1 at the end |
| `read_line` | `rdi` = buffer, `rsi` = its size | reads one line without its new line and adds a 0; `rax` = its length, or −1 at the end |

Don't mix `read_int`, `read_char` and `read_line` with your own `read` system calls: the routines read ahead and keep bytes for later.

## How they are written

The output routines all end in one helper that makes the `write` system call:

```nasm-norun
;; xenon_write: rsi = bytes, rdx = how many. Writes them all to standard output.
xenon_write:
        push    rbx
        push    r12
        mov     rbx, rsi
        mov     r12, rdx
.more:  test    r12, r12
        jle     .done
        mov     eax, 1                  ; system call 1: write
        mov     edi, [rel xenon_fd]     ; normally 1
        mov     rsi, rbx
        mov     rdx, r12
        syscall
        test    rax, rax
        jle     .done                   ; an error: give up quietly
        add     rbx, rax                ; write may do only part: carry on from there
        sub     r12, rax
        jmp     .more
.done:  pop     r12
        pop     rbx
        ret

;; print_str: rdi = the address of a zero-terminated string.
print_str:
        mov     rsi, rdi
        xor     edx, edx
.len:   cmp     byte [rsi + rdx], 0
        je      .go
        inc     rdx
        jmp     .len
.go:    jmp     xenon_write             ; a tail call: xenon_write's ret returns for us

;; print_uint: rdi = an unsigned number, printed in decimal.
print_uint:
        sub     rsp, 40
        lea     rsi, [rsp + 32]         ; digits are written backwards from here
        mov     rax, rdi
        mov     ecx, 10
.digit: xor     edx, edx
        div     rcx                     ; rax = rax / 10, rdx = the last digit
        add     dl, '0'
        dec     rsi
        mov     [rsi], dl
        test    rax, rax
        jnz     .digit
        lea     rdx, [rsp + 32]
        sub     rdx, rsi
        call    xenon_write
        add     rsp, 40
        ret

;; print_int: rdi = a signed number.
print_int:
        test    rdi, rdi
        jns     print_uint              ; not negative: print it as it is
        push    rdi
        mov     edi, '-'
        call    print_char
        pop     rdi
        neg     rdi                     ; the most negative number stays itself, and prints right as unsigned
        jmp     print_uint
```

`read_int` reads its input in 4096-byte pieces with the `read` system call, keeps a position in that buffer, and puts back the character after a number so the next read sees it. Lesson 6.02 builds the same pieces yourself.
